name: AIDA
subtitle: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action
description: This is the oldest structure in advertising and it still works for health content because it follows how a person actually changes their mind. First they notice, then they care, then they want the outcome, then they do something about it. Each stage only exists to earn the next one.

stages.name: Attention
stages.description: Open with a line that breaks the scroll. A number, a blunt statement, or a direct address to a group works better than a greeting.

stages.name: Interest
stages.description: Explain why this topic touches the viewer's own life. This is where you make it personal, not academic.

stages.name: Desire
stages.description: Show what they gain. Early detection, avoided surgery, better sleep, fewer hospital visits.

stages.name: Action
stages.description: One instruction only. Get the test done, comment the keyword, save the reel, book a consult.

example_script: Most thyroid problems in women go unnoticed for years. Tiredness, hair fall and weight gain get blamed on stress. One blood test settles it. If you have had these signs for three months, get a TSH test done this week.
pitfall_warning: AIDA slides into a sales pitch very easily. Keep the desire section medical, not promotional, otherwise the doctor starts sounding like an ad.

selection_rules.angle: actionable awareness

name: PAS
subtitle: Problem, Agitate, Solution
description: PAS works because people act on discomfort faster than on information. You name something the viewer already feels, show them where it is heading, then hand them the way out. It is the most reliable structure for anything patients quietly ignore.

stages.name: Problem
stages.description: Name the problem in the viewer's own words, not in clinical language.

stages.name: Agitate
stages.description: Explain what it becomes if left alone. Stay factual and specific.

stages.name: Solution
stages.description: Give the correct medical step, simply stated.

example_script: You take an antacid every night before sleeping. That is not a cure, it is a signal. Long term acid reflux damages the food pipe lining and can change those cells permanently. If it has been more than six weeks, you need an endoscopy, not another tablet.
pitfall_warning: The agitate step is where doctors lose credibility fastest. Describe the real consequence, never an exaggerated worst case.

selection_rules.angle: stakes escalation

name: PASA
subtitle: Problem, Agitate, Solution, Action
description: PAS with a closing instruction attached. The extra A exists because a solution alone tells the viewer what is true, while an action tells them what to do in the next ten minutes. Use it when the reel has a job beyond awareness.
best_use_cases: Educational reels that also have to generate comments

stages.name: Problem
stages.description: State the issue plainly.

stages.name: Agitate
stages.description: Raise the stakes honestly so the viewer stops scrolling past it.

stages.name: Solution
stages.description: Explain the correct approach.

stages.name: Action
stages.description: Ask for one specific thing. Do not stack three CTAs.

example_script: Your father's BP is controlled, so he stopped the tablet. BP does not stay low because of your body, it stays low because of the tablet. Stopping it silently raises stroke risk. Never stop BP medicine without your doctor. Send this reel to whoever needs to hear it at home.
pitfall_warning: One CTA per reel. Asking to comment, save and share in the same ending kills all three.

selection_rules.angle: call-to-action for loved ones

name: HPSA
subtitle: Hook, Problem, Solution, Action
description: The tightest general purpose format for short reels. It is PASA with the agitation removed, which makes it faster and calmer. When you only have thirty seconds and the topic does not need urgency, this is the default choice.
best_use_cases: Short doctor reels in the twenty to forty second range.

stages.name: Hook
stages.description: Three to five seconds. Make a claim or ask a sharp question.

stages.name: Problem
stages.description: One line naming the health issue.

stages.name: Solution
stages.description: Two or three practical points, nothing more.

stages.name: Action
stages.description: Close with the single next step.

example_script: Knee pain at forty is not old age. It is usually weak thigh muscles and extra body weight pressing on the joint. Ten minutes of straight leg raises daily and two kilos less on the scale changes it. Start with the leg raises tonight.
pitfall_warning: The temptation is to add a fourth and fifth point. Cut them. Short reels lose people at the point where the list stops feeling finishable.

selection_rules.angle: rapid 30s explainer without heavy agitation

name: Hook, Value, CTA
subtitle: The three part minimum
description: The stripped down version of every other framework. No setup, no build up, just the useful information delivered immediately. It works when the topic is genuinely simple and the viewer does not need convincing that it matters.
best_use_cases: Fast educational reels where the information itself is the whole point.

stages.name: Hook
stages.description: Open directly on the topic.

stages.name: Value
stages.description: Deliver the information with no preamble.

stages.name: CTA
stages.description: Close in one line.

example_script: Three foods that quietly raise your sugar even though they taste healthy. Fruit juice, brown bread, and flavoured yogurt. Check the label before you buy any of them. Save this for your next grocery run.
pitfall_warning: If the topic actually needs explanation, this format will feel abrupt and the reel will not hold. Use the Hook to Explanation format instead.

selection_rules.angle: zero-preamble direct value

name: Hook, Explanation, CTA
subtitle: The reason behind the symptom
description: Same shape as the previous one, but the middle is an explanation rather than a list. People remember information far better when they understand the mechanism behind it, and a doctor explaining the why is exactly what the audience came for.
best_use_cases: Doctor led educational content where understanding changes behaviour.

stages.name: Hook
stages.description: Name the symptom or the observation.

stages.name: Explanation
stages.description: Explain what is happening inside the body, in ordinary language.

stages.name: CTA
stages.description: End with the practical takeaway.

example_script: Why do your legs cramp at night? During sleep your blood flow slows and the calf muscle stays shortened for hours. Low magnesium and dehydration make it worse. Drink water before bed and stretch your calves for thirty seconds. If it happens daily, get your electrolytes checked.
pitfall_warning: Keep the explanation to one mechanism. Two mechanisms in a reel means neither one lands.

selection_rules.angle: explaining biological mechanism to drive habit change

name: Hook, Medical Explanation, Solution
subtitle: The authority format
description: This is the format that makes a doctor look like a doctor. The middle section carries real clinical reasoning, simplified but not diluted, and the ending converts that reasoning into something the viewer can do. It builds the kind of trust that turns viewers into patients.
best_use_cases: positioning a doctor as the person who actually explains things.

stages.name: Hook
stages.description: Start with the question or symptom the audience already has.

stages.name: Medical explanation
stages.description: Give the real reason. Use the correct term once, then translate it.

stages.name: Solution
stages.description: Convert the explanation into an action.

example_script: Why does your sugar reading go up in the morning even without eating? Between three and eight in the morning your body releases cortisol and growth hormone to wake you up, and both push glucose into the blood. It is called the dawn phenomenon. Shift your dinner earlier and ask your doctor about the timing of your night dose.
pitfall_warning: One technical term per reel is credibility. Four is a lecture. Say the term, then immediately say it in plain words.

selection_rules.angle: doctor clinical reasoning in plain language

name: Myth, Truth, Explanation
subtitle: Correcting what people already believe
description: Myth busting performs well because the viewer already holds the belief, so the correction feels personally relevant. The order matters. State the myth first so people recognise themselves in it, then correct it, then explain why the myth exists at all.

stages.name: Myth
stages.description: State the belief exactly as people say it.

stages.name: Truth
stages.description: Correct it in one clear sentence.

stages.name: Explanation
stages.description: Explain why the belief spread and where it is partly right.

example_script: People say curd at night causes cold. Curd does not cause cold, viruses do. The belief exists because curd is cooling and can thicken mucus slightly in someone who already has a blocked nose. If you are healthy, curd at night is completely fine.
pitfall_warning: Do not mock the belief. Half your audience holds it, and mocking them ends the reel emotionally before it ends technically.

selection_rules.angle: respectful correction of popular beliefs

name: Mistake, Consequence, Fix
subtitle: Behaviour correction
description: Aimed squarely at something the viewer is doing right now. Because it names an action rather than a condition, it produces stronger recognition than symptom content, and the fix gives them a way to resolve the discomfort immediately.

stages.name: Mistake
stages.description: Name the exact behaviour.

stages.name: Consequence
stages.description: Explain what it causes over time.

stages.name: Fix
stages.description: Give the better alternative in a single step.

example_script: Crushing tablets to swallow them easily. Many tablets have a slow release coating, and crushing dumps the full dose into your body at once. If a tablet is hard to swallow, ask your doctor for a syrup or a smaller strength instead.
pitfall_warning: Address the mistake, not the person. Say the habit is common, then correct it.

selection_rules.angle: correcting specific observable actions

name: Symptom, Possible Reason, What To Do
subtitle: The safe symptom format
description: The standard structure for symptom content, built so the doctor educates without diagnosing. The plural in possible reasons is deliberate. Listing several causes tells the viewer that a reel cannot decide their case, which is both accurate and protective.
best_use_cases: Common symptoms people search for before they see a doctor.

stages.name: Symptom
stages.description: Describe it the way a patient would describe it.

stages.name: Possible reasons
stages.description: Give two or three, ordered from most to least common.

stages.name: What to do
stages.description: State the point at which they should see someone.

example_script: Chest burning after meals is usually acid reflux, sometimes gastritis, and occasionally a heart issue in people over forty with diabetes or BP. If it comes with sweating, jaw pain or breathlessness, treat it as an emergency and go to a hospital immediately.
pitfall_warning: Never diagnose through a reel. Always give a threshold that sends them to an actual consultation.

selection_rules.angle: non-prescriptive differential education

name: Normal vs Red Flag
subtitle: Normal situation, warning sign, action
description: One of the most genuinely useful things a doctor can publish. It draws the line between what can wait and what cannot. It also calms the anxious viewer while catching the one who is actually in danger, which is why these reels get forwarded within families.
best_use_cases: anything where timing decides the outcome.

stages.name: Normal
stages.description: Describe the version that does not need panic.

stages.name: Red flag
stages.description: List the specific signs that change the picture.

stages.name: Action
stages.description: Say exactly what to do and how fast.

example_script: A fever for two or three days with body pain is usually viral and settles on its own. Bleeding gums, black stools, severe stomach pain or a sudden drop in urine are not viral fever signs. In dengue season, those four mean you go to a hospital the same day.
pitfall_warning: Red flags must be specific and countable. Vague warnings like feeling unwell make the whole reel useless.

selection_rules.angle: urgent boundary between waiting and rushing to hospital

name: Fear, Explanation, Reassurance, Solution
subtitle: Handling serious topics responsibly
description: Serious topics need attention without panic. The reassurance step is what separates this from fear mongering. You acknowledge the risk, explain the mechanism, tell the viewer it is manageable, then show them how. Skipping reassurance leaves people scared and passive, which changes nothing.

stages.name: Fear
stages.description: Name the real risk honestly.

stages.name: Explanation
stages.description: Explain the medical reason behind it.

stages.name: Reassurance
stages.description: State what is in the patient's control.

stages.name: Solution
stages.description: Give the concrete next step.

example_script: Kidneys can lose most of their function before you feel anything. It happens because the remaining tissue compensates until it cannot. The reassuring part is that a creatinine test costs very little and catches it early. If you have diabetes or BP, do that test once a year.
pitfall_warning: Never end on the fear. A reel that raises alarm and gives no next step does harm.

selection_rules.angle: defusing panic with clinical explanation and actionable reassurance

name: Question, Answer, Explanation
subtitle: Direct answer first
description: Answer first, explain second. This runs against how doctors are trained to speak, and that is exactly why it works on social media. The viewer gets what they came for in the first five seconds and stays for the reasoning instead of waiting for it.
best_use_cases: Frequently asked questions and recurring patient doubts.

stages.name: Question
stages.description: Ask it exactly as patients ask it.

stages.name: Answer
stages.description: Yes, no, or the direct number. No hedging.

stages.name: Explanation
stages.description: Give the reasoning and the exception.

example_script: Can a diabetic eat rice? Yes. The problem is quantity and what is on the plate with it. One cup of rice with dal, vegetables and curd raises sugar far less than two cups with a light curry. Fill half the plate with vegetables and the rice takes care of itself.
pitfall_warning: If the honest answer is it depends, say what it depends on within the same breath. Never leave the viewer without an answer.

selection_rules.angle: immediate definitive answer followed by practical nuance

name: Patient Question, Doctor Answer
subtitle: Consultation style
description: Structurally similar to the previous framework, but performed as a two person exchange. The value is emotional rather than informational. The viewer watches someone like them ask the thing they were embarrassed to ask, and gets to hear the answer without having to ask it.

stages.name: Patient
stages.description: Ask a natural, slightly hesitant question.

stages.name: Doctor
stages.description: Answer directly and without judgement.

stages.name: Explanation
stages.description: Add the short medical reason.

stages.name: Guidance
stages.description: Close with what the patient should do.

example_script: Doctor, I stopped my thyroid tablet because I felt fine. That feeling fine is the tablet working. Thyroid hormone does not restart on its own once the gland has stopped. Restart it and get your TSH checked in six weeks.
pitfall_warning: The patient line has to sound like a real person. Scripted patient dialogue is obvious within two seconds and it takes the doctor's credibility down with it.

selection_rules.angle: two-person supportive bedside consultation

name: What Happens If
subtitle: Consequence question, explanation, prevention
description: Opens on curiosity rather than a problem. Because the hook is a question about consequences, the viewer stays to find out what happens to their own body. It suits habits people know are questionable but have never seen explained.

stages.name: What happens if
stages.description: Ask the consequence question about a common habit.

stages.name: Explanation
stages.description: Describe what actually happens inside the body.

stages.name: Prevention
stages.description: Give the correction.

example_script: What happens if you skip breakfast every day? Your body pulls glucose from stored reserves and raises cortisol to keep you functioning, which is why you get irritable by eleven and overeat at lunch. If mornings are rushed, keep it small. Curd, a banana, a handful of nuts.
pitfall_warning: Describe the process, not just the outcome. The inside the body part is what makes this format memorable.

selection_rules.angle: curiosity-driven internal bodily mechanism

name: 3 Signs
subtitle: The high save format
description: Three is the number the format lives on. Two feels incomplete, five stops feeling checkable, three is what a person can hold in their head while thinking about their own family. This is consistently one of the strongest performing structures in health content.
best_use_cases: Early detection topics and anything a viewer will check against a parent or spouse.

stages.name: Hook
stages.description: Name the condition and the number.

stages.name: Three signs
stages.description: Deliver them fast, one line each.

stages.name: Meaning
stages.description: Say what the combination may indicate.

stages.name: Next step
stages.description: Tell them what to do if they recognised two or more.

example_script: Three signs your liver is under stress. Constant tiredness after meals. Puffiness around the eyes in the morning. Pale or unusually dark stools. Any two of these together deserve a liver function test.
pitfall_warning: Keep it at three. The moment you say and one bonus sign, the format loses the tightness that made it work.

selection_rules.angle: countable three-sign checkable triage

name: 3 Mistakes
subtitle: Recognition through error
description: The same rhythm as three signs, aimed at behaviour instead of symptoms. It performs well because viewers recognise themselves in at least one mistake, and that recognition is what drives the comment and the share.

stages.name: Topic
stages.description: Set up the area in one line.

stages.name: Three mistakes
stages.description: Name each one as an action people take.

stages.name: Takeaway
stages.description: Close with one principle that covers all three.

example_script: Three mistakes people make with BP tablets. Taking it only when the reading is high. Stopping it after a good report. Taking it at a different time every day. Blood pressure medicine works on consistency, not on readings.
pitfall_warning: The three mistakes should not be variations of the same mistake. If they overlap, the reel feels padded.

selection_rules.angle: three distinct behavioral blunders unified by one principle

name: Do This, Not That
subtitle: Swap based correction
description: Instead of telling people to stop something, you give them a replacement. Removal creates resistance while substitution feels achievable, and the contrast makes the reel easy to follow visually as well as verbally.
best_use_cases: Habit corrections where the underlying need is legitimate.

stages.name: Not that
stages.description: Name the common habit.

stages.name: Do this
stages.description: Give the direct replacement.

stages.name: Why
stages.description: One line on the difference it makes.

example_script: Do not drink tea immediately after a meal. Wait an hour. Tannins in tea block iron absorption from your food, and in a country where anaemia is this common, that one hour matters more than people think.
pitfall_warning: The replacement must be realistic for the audience. Telling people to swap rice for quinoa is advice nobody follows.

selection_rules.angle: achievable substitution rather than restrictive elimination

name: If You Are X, Watch This
subtitle: Audience calling
description: Opens by naming a group so precisely that everyone outside it scrolls on and everyone inside it stops. Narrowing the audience deliberately raises the completion rate among the people who actually matter for that topic.
best_use_cases: gender specific or condition specific advice.

stages.name: Call the audience
stages.description: Name the group in the first two seconds.

stages.name: Their issue
stages.description: State the problem specific to them.

stages.name: Two or three points
stages.description: Keep it to what applies only to this group.

stages.name: Action
stages.description: Close with their next step.

example_script: If you are a woman over thirty five in an office job, this is for you. You are in the highest risk group for vitamin D deficiency and low iron at the same time. Get both tested together, not separately, and take iron away from your calcium.
pitfall_warning: The narrower the group, the better this works. Broad calls like if you are an adult defeat the entire purpose.

selection_rules.angle: opening scroll-stopper naming an exact demographic

name: Doctor Reacts
subtitle: Responding to a claim
description: Borrows attention from something already circulating. Because the claim has done the work of getting people interested, the doctor only has to supply the correction. Reaction content also positions the doctor as a filter people can trust, which has value beyond any single reel.

stages.name: The claim
stages.description: Show or state it clearly.

stages.name: Reaction
stages.description: React honestly. Sometimes the claim is partly right, and saying so builds more trust than dismissing it.

stages.name: Correction
stages.description: State what is actually true.

stages.name: Explanation
stages.description: Give the medical reasoning.

example_script: A reel says drinking warm water with lemon burns belly fat. It does not burn fat. What it does is fill your stomach before a meal so you eat less, and that is the entire effect. The lemon is not doing anything to your fat cells.
pitfall_warning: Do not name and attack individual creators. React to the claim, not the person, and keep it about the medicine.

selection_rules.angle: objective medical filter dissecting trending claims

name: Story, Lesson, CTA
subtitle: Personal branding through cases
description: The strongest format for making a doctor feel like a human being. A short account of something seen in practice carries emotional weight that a list of facts cannot, and the lesson lands because the viewer arrived at it through a person rather than a rule.

stages.name: Story
stages.description: One short situation. Keep it to two or three sentences.

stages.name: Lesson
stages.description: Draw out the health point.

stages.name: CTA
stages.description: Close with what the viewer should do differently.

example_script: A man in his forties came in for a knee problem. His BP reading during the routine check was 190. He had no symptoms at all and had never tested it. He walked in for his knee and walked out on BP medication. Check your BP once a year even when nothing is wrong.
pitfall_warning: Never include anything that could identify a patient. Change the details, avoid photographs, and do not name the hospital or the date.

selection_rules.angle: empathetic real-world patient vignette teaching a universal lesson

name: Curiosity Gap
subtitle: Withholding the answer
description: Opens with something incomplete or counterintuitive so the viewer keeps watching to close the gap in their own head. The gap has to be small enough to be resolved inside the reel, otherwise it reads as clickbait and the audience learns not to trust the account.
best_use_cases: Improving retention on topics that would otherwise sound routine.

stages.name: Open the gap
stages.description: Say something surprising or unfinished.

stages.name: Delay
stages.description: Add one line of context, no more.

stages.name: Reveal
stages.description: Deliver the answer clearly.

stages.name: Takeaway
stages.description: Close with what it means for them.

example_script: The most common reason for morning headaches has nothing to do with your head. It is your breathing at night. Untreated sleep apnoea drops your oxygen repeatedly through the night and you wake up with a dull headache and no memory of why. If you snore heavily, get a sleep study.
pitfall_warning: Always close the gap. An unanswered hook feels like a trick and costs you the next reel's attention.

selection_rules.angle: unresolved opening puzzle resolved before the end

name: Open Loop
subtitle: Answer held to the end
description: A longer form of the curiosity gap. You raise a question at the start and release information in pieces, keeping the central answer for the final seconds. It is the strongest structure for watch time and the easiest one to overplay.
best_use_cases: Longer reels of forty five to ninety seconds where you need people to stay to the end.

stages.name: Open the loop
stages.description: Pose the question or the incomplete idea.

stages.name: Feed in pieces
stages.description: Give useful information along the way so the wait is earned.

stages.name: Hold the answer
stages.description: Keep the main point for late in the reel.

stages.name: Close the loop
stages.description: Answer it explicitly before the reel ends.

example_script: There is one blood test most people over forty have never done, and it predicts heart risk better than cholesterol. Not sugar. Not the standard lipid profile. It is Lipoprotein(a), it is largely genetic, and a normal cholesterol report tells you nothing about it. Ask for it once. The value does not change through your life.
pitfall_warning: The information you give while holding the answer must be useful on its own. Filler in the middle is where viewers leave.

selection_rules.angle: progressive clue release with delayed climactic reveal

name: Pattern Interrupt
subtitle: Contradicting the expected
description: Opens by stating the opposite of what the audience assumes a doctor will say. The contradiction creates a small jolt that stops the scroll, and the rest of the reel resolves it. Used well it is memorable. Used often it makes a doctor sound contrarian.
best_use_cases: Widely repeated advice that is oversimplified or wrong.

stages.name: Interrupt
stages.description: State the surprising position directly.

stages.name: Why
stages.description: Explain the reasoning immediately. Do not make people wait.

stages.name: Correct view
stages.description: Give the accurate, complete picture.

example_script: Stop counting ten thousand steps. The number came from a Japanese pedometer advertisement, not from research. Studies show most of the benefit arrives between four and seven thousand steps a day. Walk at a pace where talking is slightly difficult, and stop worrying about the number.
pitfall_warning: The interrupt must be defensible. Saying something shocking that you then have to walk back damages trust more than a boring hook ever would.

selection_rules.angle: direct immediate contradiction of dogma with defensible science

name: Listicle
subtitle: Numbered points
description: The most predictable structure and the most saveable. Announcing the number tells the viewer exactly how long the reel will feel, which makes them more likely to start it. Its weakness is that it carries no reasoning, so use it where the points are self explanatory.

stages.name: Hook
stages.description: State the number and the topic together.

stages.name: Points
stages.description: One line each, in the same rhythm.

stages.name: Takeaway
stages.description: One closing line that ties them together.

stages.name: CTA
stages.description: Ask for the save.

example_script: Five questions to ask before any surgery. What happens if I do not do this. How many of these have you done. What is the recovery time. What are the chances I will need a second one. What will the total cost be including everything. Save this before your next appointment.
pitfall_warning: Four to six points is the range. Beyond that, break it into two reels.

selection_rules.angle: rhythmic 4-to-6 point self-explanatory list

name: Comparison
subtitle: X vs Y
description: Built for the moment a patient is standing in front of two options and does not know the difference. Comparison content ranks well in search and gets saved often because it answers a decision rather than a curiosity.

stages.name: Introduce both
stages.description: Name them and say why people confuse them.

stages.name: Key differences
stages.description: Two or three differences that actually matter to a patient.

stages.name: When each matters
stages.description: Say which situation calls for which.

stages.name: Takeaway
stages.description: Give the practical rule.

example_script: Migraine or sinus headache. Migraine is usually one sided, worsens with light and sound, and comes with nausea. Sinus pain sits over the cheeks and forehead, worsens when you bend forward, and comes with a blocked nose. Most people treating sinusitis for years are actually treating migraines.
pitfall_warning: Compare on differences a patient can observe themselves. Comparisons based on lab findings are useless in a reel.

selection_rules.angle: observable side-by-side patient differentiation

name: Cause, Effect, Prevention
subtitle: The preventive chain
description: Shows the full arc from what starts a problem to what it becomes to how it is stopped. It is the clearest way to explain why prevention is worth the effort, because the viewer sees the chain rather than being told to trust it.

stages.name: Cause
stages.description: Name what starts it.

stages.name: Effect
stages.description: Show what it leads to over years, not days.

stages.name: Prevention
stages.description: Give the intervention and where in the chain it works.

example_script: Sitting for nine hours a day slows the enzyme that clears fat from your blood. Over years that shows up as higher triglycerides, insulin resistance and belly fat, even in people who look thin. Standing and walking for three minutes every hour restores most of that enzyme activity. The frequency matters more than the duration.
pitfall_warning: Give a realistic timescale. Effects stated without a time frame sound like scare tactics.

selection_rules.angle: multi-year causal chain leading to realistic micro-intervention

name: Why Framework
subtitle: Why does this happen, explanation, advice
description: Takes something the viewer has experienced and never questioned, and explains the mechanism. It plays directly to a doctor's advantage, because explaining the body is the one thing an audience cannot get from anyone else in their feed.
best_use_cases: Everyday physical experiences with a clean scientific explanation.

stages.name: Why
stages.description: Ask the question the viewer has had but never looked up.

stages.name: Explanation
stages.description: Explain the mechanism in ordinary language.

stages.name: Advice
stages.description: Close with the practical implication.

example_script: Why do you feel sleepy right after lunch? Blood flow shifts towards digestion and a heavy carbohydrate meal spikes insulin, which pushes tryptophan into the brain and raises serotonin. A lighter lunch with protein and a ten minute walk after eating removes most of it.
pitfall_warning: Simplify without inventing. If the honest mechanism is complicated, explain the part that is true rather than a neat version that is not.

selection_rules.angle: clean scientific explanation of an unexamined daily sensation

name: Checklist
subtitle: Built for saves
description: Made to be returned to rather than watched once. The value is not in the explanation but in the completeness, so the viewer keeps it for a moment that has not arrived yet. This is the highest saving format in health content.

stages.name: Introduce
stages.description: Say what the checklist is for and when they will need it.

stages.name: Points
stages.description: Short, concrete, in the order they will be used.

stages.name: Save prompt
stages.description: Ask directly for the save and give the reason.

example_script: What to carry for a first consultation. Previous prescriptions, not a summary of them. All reports in date order. A list of every tablet you take including supplements. Your family history of diabetes, BP and heart disease. Save this. It will cut your consultation time in half.
pitfall_warning: Every point must be something the viewer can physically do or carry. Vague items break the usefulness of a checklist.

selection_rules.angle: concrete physical checklist intended for future reference

name: Before, After, Bridge
subtitle: Showing the change
description: Starts in the viewer's current situation, shows them a better one, then explains the single change that connects the two. The bridge is the whole point. Without a specific and believable bridge, this becomes a motivational reel and delivers nothing.

stages.name: Before
stages.description: Describe the current state in recognisable detail.

stages.name: After
stages.description: Describe the realistic improved state.

stages.name: Bridge
stages.description: Name the one change that makes the difference.

example_script: Right now you wake up tired even after seven hours of sleep. It is possible to wake up before the alarm and feel clear. The change is not more sleep, it is a fixed wake up time, including on Sundays. Your body clock cannot stabilise if the schedule moves every weekend.
pitfall_warning: Keep the after honest. Overpromising in health content is the fastest way to lose the audience you spent months earning.

selection_rules.angle: relatable baseline transformed through a single credible bridge
